text: Dinner's DONE! The little red button popped!
That button popped twenty minutes ago. Your turkey is overcooked.
The button would never lie to me.
The button has been lying to America for decades.
My whole family is coming. Like, all of them. Aunt Linda is coming.
Fine. By the end of this, your dinner will beat the button, the pie, the gravy, and Aunt Linda.
Easy. I don't need a recipe. I have instincts.
Your instincts are why we're here. I'm keeping score.
Score of what?
Every time you're wrong. Starting now.
Step one, the turkey. You cook it till it's done. Boom. Chapter over.
Done is a temperature, not a feeling. The USDA says one sixty-five in the thickest part of the breast, the thigh, and the wing.
Wait, the whole bird isn't the same temperature?
Nope. A turkey is two meats wearing one coat. White meat in the breast, dark meat in the legs.

The breast is lean. Push it much past one sixty-five and it dries out. The thighs are full of connective tissue, and they actually get better around one seventy to one seventy-five, when that tissue melts into gelatin.
So the turkey wants two different temperatures at the same time?
Like every family at this table. Yes.
Why is the leg meat even dark? Did it get a tan?
No tan. Legs do the walking. Muscles that work all day need oxygen on hand, so they're packed with a protein called myoglobin, and myoglobin is red.
The breast barely works, since turkeys hardly fly. Less myoglobin, paler meat, and less fat to protect it. That's why it dries out first.
So the breast is lazy and the legs are athletes.
Exactly. And in the oven, the lazy part is on top, closest to the heat.
Can we just... flip the turkey's whole life around?
Kind of. You can spatchcock it. Cut out the backbone and press the bird flat, so the legs sit out at the edges where it's hottest and the breast lies flat and thin.
Everything cooks more evenly, and a lot faster. It's the closest thing to fixing the two-temperature problem.
Spatchcock. That's my new favorite word.
Then that's why the button is genius. It knows.
Let me show you the button. Inside, there's a spring, pushed down and held by a tiny blob of soft metal.
When that metal gets hot enough, it melts, lets go of the spring, and the red stick shoots up. The idea came from fire sprinklers, which work the same way.
And it melts at one sixty-five, right?
Most of them are set to pop around one eighty to one eighty-five. By then the breast is way past one sixty-five. That's your dry turkey.
I trusted that button with my life.
And there's a second trap. When you take a turkey out of the oven, it keeps cooking. The outside is still hotter than the middle, so heat keeps moving inward.
A big roast can climb another ten degrees or more while it rests. So if you pull it right at one sixty-five, you're actually serving it hotter.
So the turkey cooks itself on the counter?
Basically. Use a real thermometer, pull it a little early, and let it rest under foil. The rest also lets the juices settle, so they end up in the meat, not on the cutting board.
Thermometer. Rest. Ignore the button. I'm a genius.
You're a genius who was wrong three times in one chapter.
Fine. But the turkey's the hard part, right?
The turkey isn't even the hardest thing on this table.
Fine, but the turkey's still frozen. I'll leave it on the counter tonight. Thawed by morning.
Thawed on the outside. Still an iceberg in the middle.
Bacteria grow fastest between forty and one forty degrees. On the counter, the outside sits in that zone for hours while the inside is still frozen solid.
So my turkey is a bacteria hotel.
All-inclusive. Thaw it in the fridge. The USDA says about one day for every four to five pounds. A big bird needs most of a week.
A week? Thanksgiving is in, like, a few days!
Then do it in cold water, sealed in the bag, and change the water every thirty minutes. Roughly half an hour per pound.
Phew. Then I'll stuff it the night before, so it's ready to go.
Two problems. Stuffing soaks up raw turkey juice. To be safe, the stuffing in the middle has to hit one sixty-five too.
And the middle of the bird is the last place to heat up. By the time the stuffing is safe, the breast is way overcooked again.
The turkey keeps setting traps.
So bake the stuffing in its own dish. It gets crispy edges, and nobody gets sick.
What about brining? My neighbor soaks his turkey in a bucket of salt water.
Your neighbor is onto something. Salt loosens some of the muscle proteins, so the meat holds on to more water while it cooks. Juicier breast, and a little more room for error.
So salt is basically turkey insurance.
Salt is turkey insurance. The button is a scam.
The pie, then. Pie is easy. You put pie in the oven until it looks like pie.
Pumpkin pie isn't really a cake. It's a custard. Eggs, milk, pumpkin. The eggs are what make it set.
Set like jelly?
Kind of. When egg proteins heat up, they unravel and link into a soft net that holds the filling together. That's the smooth, creamy slice.
But if they keep heating, that net keeps tightening. It squeezes, it shrinks, and the top splits right down the middle.
That's why grandma's pie always has the Grand Canyon in it.
Respectfully, yes. The fix feels wrong: pull the pie while the center still wobbles a little. The edges should look set, the middle should jiggle like soft gel.
Just like the turkey, the heat keeps moving into the center after it leaves the oven. The wobble finishes on its own as it cools.
Taking it out when it looks unfinished? That's terrifying.
That's baking.
And the bottom?  Mine is always soggy. Like a wet napkin.
Wet filling poured into raw dough soaks in before the crust has a chance to set. So bake the empty crust first, then add the filling. It's called blind baking.
Blind baking. Sounds dangerous. I love it.
It's baking with the lights on. You just weigh the empty crust down so it doesn't puff up.
Got it. Wobble, blind bake. And to be safe, I'll leave it in a little longer.
That's the exact thing that cracks it.
The sides! Gravy first. I'll just dump flour in the hot pan juice. Thick gravy, instant.
Instant lumps. Flour is starch. When dry starch hits hot liquid, the outside of each clump turns to gel right away and seals dry flour inside. Tiny flour dumplings.
Gravy dumplings sound kind of amazing.

They taste like raw flour. The fix is to split the starch up before it gets hot. Whisk it into cold liquid first, or cook it in the fat first, like a roux. Every grain gets its own space, so it thickens smooth.
Fine. Then mashed potatoes. I'll use the blender. Maximum smooth.
Maximum glue. Potato cells are little bags of starch. Cooking makes the starch swell. A few burst cells make it creamy.
But a blender bursts almost all of them. All that loose starch turns into a sticky, stretchy paste. You made wallpaper paste.
My potatoes are wallpaper?
Your potatoes could hold up wallpaper. Mash gently, by hand, and stop when it's smooth.
And the cranberry sauce? How does that wiggle without any gelatin?
Cranberries are packed with pectin, the same stuff that sets jam. Cook them with sugar and the pectin builds a gel on its own.
The cranberries brought their own Jell-O.
Pretty much. Now for the part everyone blames on the turkey.
Why is everyone asleep? Even Aunt Linda. It's the turkey, right? Tryptophan.
Turkey has about the same tryptophan as chicken. Nobody blames chicken for their nap.
Then who did this?
The meal did. A typical Thanksgiving dinner can run around three thousand calories, heavy on carbs: potatoes, stuffing, rolls, pie.
Digesting that much food takes work, and a carb-heavy feast plus a long day is what knocks people out. The turkey is just the face of the crime.
Then why do I only get sleepy on Thanksgiving?
Because it's the one day you eat three dinners in a row, sit on a couch for six hours, and argue about football. Any one of those would do it.
And the tryptophan in turkey has to compete with a bunch of other amino acids to get into your brain. It's not some sleepy power-up.
So the turkey's innocent.
The turkey is the only one at this table who didn't lie to you.
Wait. Let me run it back. Thaw it in the fridge. Brine it. Stuffing in its own dish.
Yep.
Thermometer, not the button. Pull it a little early and rest it.
Yep.
Pull the pie while it still wobbles. Blind bake the crust.
Yep.
Cold whisk for the gravy. Gentle mash. And the cranberries bring their own Jell-O.
And a smaller first plate if you want to stay awake for the game.
I am the Thanksgiving master. How many times was I wrong?
Let's check the counter.
That's not a score. That's a phone number.
Next week, you're fixing your car. And now you know.
